intro: This unit slows down. Earlier units walked through the whole Bible; this one stays inside the four gospels and reads a few chapters closely. First comes the teaching of Jesus: the long sermon in Matthew 5–7, its shorter cousin in Luke 6, and the parables, short stories that end with a turn. Then come the last chapters of each gospel, the Passion narratives, which describe one Friday four times, and the accounts of an empty tomb.

Close reading means noticing. Which gospel says "the poor" and which says "the poor in spirit"? Which manuscripts end Mark at 16:8? What does Luke's Jesus say from the cross that John's does not? Every difference is evidence of what a writer chose, and every reader, Jewish, Christian, Muslim, secular, brings a way of reading. This unit teaches you to name the text, the writer, the manuscript and the reader before you say what a passage means.

By the end you will be able to compare parallel gospel passages, explain how a parable works, describe what historians can and cannot say about Jesus of Nazareth, and state how Jewish, Christian and Muslim traditions each understand him, without deciding for anyone which is right. That is the skill a public school can teach, and it is a skill you can use on any text.
bigQuestion: How can a reader study the sayings, stories and death of Jesus closely, as history and literature, while respecting the many ways they are believed?

title: Reading the Gospels Closely

chapters.title: The Sermon on the Mount and the Parables
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the Gospels present the teaching of Jesus, and why do so many of his sayings and stories end in a surprise?

story.title: A Question Answered With a Story
story.kicker: A legal expert asks for a definition and gets a road, a wounded man and three travelers instead.
paragraphs: Luke 10 sets the scene. A man the text calls a lawyer, an expert in the Torah, the law of Moses, stands up to test a traveling teacher named Jesus. He asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus turns the question back: what does the law say? The lawyer answers with two commands from his own scriptures: love God with all your heart (Deuteronomy 6:5) and love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus tells him he has answered well.

Then the lawyer asks a second question, and Luke says he asked it to justify himself: "And who is my neighbor?" It is a fair question. A word like neighbor needs edges. Does it mean the person next door, a fellow Israelite, anyone at all? A teacher could have given a definition. This teacher does not. He tells a story.

A man walks the steep road down from Jerusalem to Jericho. Robbers beat him, strip him and leave him half dead. A priest comes by, sees him, and passes on the other side. A Levite, a temple worker, does the same. Then a Samaritan comes. Samaritans and Jews in the first century were neighbors who did not get along; each side saw the other as worshiping wrongly. The Samaritan stops, bandages the wounds, lifts the man onto his own animal, pays an innkeeper and promises to come back.

Jesus does not answer the lawyer's question. He asks a different one: which of these three was a neighbor to the man who was robbed? The lawyer cannot bring himself to say the word Samaritan. He says, "the one who showed mercy." Jesus says: go and do the same. The question "who counts as my neighbor?" has been replaced by "how do I act as one?"

This chapter reads the teaching of Jesus the way the lawyer heard it: as sayings and stories that refuse to sit still. We start with the long sermon in Matthew 5–7, compare it with Luke's shorter version, and then study the parable as a form. Along the way we set Jesus beside a Jewish teacher of the same era, Hillel, whose sayings sound strikingly close.
story.think: Why might a teacher answer a request for a definition with a story? What can a story do that a definition cannot?

lessons.title: A Mountain and Nine Blessings
lessons.mainIdea: Matthew 5–7 gathers the teaching of Jesus into one long sermon, and it opens with the Beatitudes, nine blessings that reverse everyday ideas of who is fortunate.
reading: The *Gospel* of Matthew is one of four books in the New Testament that tell the life of Jesus. In Matthew 5:1–2 Jesus sees the crowds, goes up a mountain, sits down, and begins to teach. Chapters 5, 6 and 7 form one continuous speech. Readers have called it the *Sermon on the Mount* since at least the fourth century; the name is not in the text. Many scholars think Matthew collected sayings that Jesus gave on many occasions and arranged them here, because Luke scatters the same sayings across his book.

The setting matters. In the Hebrew Bible, Moses receives the law on a mountain, Mount Sinai (Exodus 19–20). Matthew, whose gospel quotes the Hebrew scriptures more than any other, puts Jesus on a mountain to teach about the law. Many Christian and academic readers see a deliberate echo: Jesus is presented as a teacher who interprets the law of Moses, not as one who throws it away. Matthew 5:17 has Jesus say he came to fulfill the law, not to destroy it.

The sermon opens with the *Beatitudes*, from the Latin word for blessed. Each sentence has the same shape: "Blessed are the [kind of person], for [what they will receive]." Matthew lists nine: the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, those persecuted for righteousness, and those insulted for Jesus's sake. The rewards are the kingdom of heaven, comfort, the earth, being filled, mercy, seeing God, being called God's children.

Notice the reversal. A first-century audience, like a modern one, would expect the fortunate to be the rich, the strong and the comfortable. The Beatitudes name the mourning and the meek instead. Christians have read them in many ways: as a description of the ideal disciple, as promises for the world to come, or as a portrait of Jesus himself. The Beatitudes also echo Psalm 37:11, where the meek inherit the land, which shows the sermon drawing on the Hebrew Bible from its first lines.

words.d: one of the four New Testament books (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) that tell the life and teaching of Jesus; the word means good news
the long speech of Jesus in Matthew chapters 5 to 7; the name was given by later readers
the nine blessings that open the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3–12), each beginning "Blessed are"

look.title: Three of the Beatitudes
look.text: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
look.prompt: Each blessing names a kind of person and a reward. Which of these rewards sounds like something in this life, and which sounds like something in a life to come? What in the wording makes you think so?

check.q: Where in the New Testament is the Sermon on the Mount found?
check.why: The Sermon on the Mount is the continuous speech in Matthew chapters 5, 6 and 7. Luke 15 holds parables, Mark 4 the sower, and John 18–19 the passion.

check.q: Why do many scholars think Matthew arranged sayings from different occasions into one sermon?
choices: Because the sermon is written in Latin
Because Luke places many of the same sayings in scattered places
Because Mark says Jesus never spoke on mountains
Because the Beatitudes come from Psalm 37
check.why: The same sayings appear spread across Luke's gospel, which suggests Matthew gathered them. The sermon is in Greek, not Latin, and Mark makes no such claim.

check.q: Which figure from the Hebrew Bible do many readers hear echoed when Matthew puts Jesus on a mountain to teach about the law?
check.why: Moses received the law on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19–20). Many readers see Matthew presenting Jesus as an interpreter of that law from a mountain.

lessons.title: You Have Heard, But I Say
lessons.mainIdea: In six sayings called the antitheses, Matthew's Jesus quotes a command from the Torah and then pushes it inward, from the act to the intention behind it.
reading: Matthew 5:21–48 contains six sayings with the same pattern. Each begins "You have heard that it was said," quotes a command or a common reading of one, and continues "but I say to you." Scholars call them the *antitheses*, from a Greek word for setting one thing against another. The six topics are murder, adultery, divorce, oaths, retaliation and love of enemies. The first quotation is the commandment against murder (Exodus 20:13). Jesus adds that anger at a brother and insulting words are also answerable to judgment.

The word antithesis can mislead. In most of the six, Jesus does not cancel the command; he extends it. Not killing becomes not hating. Not committing adultery becomes not looking with lust. "An eye for an eye" (Exodus 21:24), a law that limited revenge to equal measure, becomes turning the other cheek. Many scholars note that Jewish teachers of the period also read commands this way, asking what a law is for and building a *fence* of stricter practice around it. Read like that, the sermon sits inside Jewish debate, not outside it.

The sixth antithesis is the one readers quote most. Matthew 5:43–44 has Jesus say, "You have heard that it was said, love your neighbor and hate your enemy; but I say to you, love your enemies." The command to love the neighbor is Leviticus 19:18. The words "hate your enemy" appear nowhere in the Hebrew Bible; they may reflect a popular saying or the attitude of some groups of the time. Jewish readers have pointed this out, and careful Christian readers agree that Jesus is not quoting the Torah at that point.

The section ends at 5:48: be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect. Christians have argued for centuries about how to live these sayings. Some have taken them as rules for every believer; historic peace churches such as the Mennonites refuse military service because of them. Others have read them as ideals that show how far everyone falls short, or as rules for a future kingdom. The text itself gives no instructions on how literally to take it.

words.d: the six "you have heard... but I say" sayings in Matthew 5:21–48; each quotes a command and then extends it
the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, which contain the law of Moses; also called the Pentateuch
in Jewish tradition, a stricter practice built around a command so that the command itself is never broken

look.title: A Command and Its Extension
look.text: Command (Exodus 21:24, paraphrased): an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. Saying (Matthew 5:39, paraphrased): do not resist an evil person; if someone strikes your right cheek, turn the other one too. Many historians say the older law was itself a limit: revenge could not exceed the injury. The saying goes further and asks the injured person to give up revenge altogether.
look.prompt: Is the second text canceling the first or carrying its purpose further? Write one sentence defending each reading, then say which fits the pattern of the other antitheses.

check.q: What pattern do the six antitheses share?
choices: A parable followed by its explanation
A question from a disciple and Jesus's answer
A blessing followed by a reward
"You have heard that it was said... but I say to you"
check.why: Each antithesis quotes a command with "you have heard that it was said" and extends it with "but I say to you." Blessings and rewards are the Beatitudes.

check.q: The command "love your neighbor as yourself" comes from which book?
check.why: Leviticus 19:18 is the source. Matthew quotes it; the other books do not contain that command.

check.q: How does Matthew 5:21–22 handle the commandment against murder?
choices: It says the commandment no longer applies
It replaces it with a commandment against theft
It extends it to cover anger and insulting words
It limits it to enemies in wartime
check.why: Jesus keeps the command and reaches inward: anger and insults are also answerable to judgment. The command is extended, not canceled.

lessons.title: The Prayer in Two Versions
lessons.mainIdea: The Lord's Prayer appears in Matthew 6 and, in a shorter form, in Luke 11; comparing them shows how the gospels shaped the same words and how manuscripts changed over time.
reading: Matthew 6 turns from the law to religious practice: giving, praying and fasting. The text warns against doing each one to be seen. In the middle sits a short model prayer, Matthew 6:9–13, which Christians call the *Lord's Prayer* or, from its first words in Latin, the Pater Noster. It addresses God as father, asks that God's name be honored and God's kingdom come, and then asks for bread, forgiveness and rescue from testing. Matthew's version has seven petitions, requests, in about sixty Greek words.

Luke 11:2–4 gives the same prayer in a different setting and a shorter form. In Luke a disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray, as John the Baptist taught his followers. Luke's prayer has five petitions and begins simply, "Father." Most scholars think the two versions descend from one prayer that Jesus taught in Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee, and that each gospel recorded it as its own community prayed it. Neither version is a quotation of the other.

Manuscripts add another layer. The closing line that most Protestants say, "for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever," called the *doxology*, is missing from the oldest surviving manuscripts of Matthew. Scribes seem to have added it from church practice. The King James Version (1611) includes it because the manuscripts its translators used included it; most modern translations put it in a footnote. Catholics traditionally end the prayer before the doxology, which is why the versions said in different churches differ.

The prayer's ideas are Jewish ideas. Calling God father, asking that God's name be sanctified and that God's kingdom come, all have parallels in Jewish prayers such as the Kaddish, which asks that God's great name be made holy and that God's kingdom be established. Scholars do not agree on which prayer came first, or whether both draw on common language. What is clear is that the Lord's Prayer, said daily by Christians around the world, is built from the prayer language of first-century Judaism.

words.d: the model prayer Jesus gives in Matthew 6:9–13 and Luke 11:2–4; Christians recite it in worship
a short sentence of praise added at the end of a prayer or hymn; the Lord's Prayer's doxology is absent from the oldest manuscripts
the everyday language of Galilee and Judea in the first century, related to Hebrew; most scholars think Jesus spoke it
a Jewish prayer in Aramaic that praises God's name and asks for God's kingdom; said in synagogue services

look.title: The Prayer as the King James Version Prints It
look.text: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.
look.prompt: Underline the requests that are about God and the requests that are about the people praying. Which comes first, and what might that order be meant to teach?

check.q: Which gospel gives the shorter version of the Lord's Prayer, beginning simply "Father"?
check.why: Luke 11:2–4 has five petitions and opens with "Father." Matthew 6:9–13 has seven. Mark and John do not include the prayer.

check.q: Why do most modern translations put the closing doxology of the Lord's Prayer in a footnote?
choices: It is written in Aramaic rather than Greek
The oldest manuscripts of Matthew do not contain it
It was first written in the King James Version
check.why: The doxology is missing from the oldest surviving manuscripts, so scholars think scribes added it later. The KJV printed it because its manuscripts had it.

check.q: Which Jewish prayer asks that God's name be made holy and God's kingdom be established, in language that parallels the Lord's Prayer?
check.why: The Kaddish asks that God's great name be sanctified and God's kingdom come, close to the opening petitions of the Lord's Prayer.

lessons.title: The Golden Rule and Two Houses
lessons.mainIdea: The sermon closes with a one-line summary of the law, the golden rule, and a parable of two builders that asks the hearer to act on what was heard.
reading: Matthew 7:12 gives a single sentence that readers have called the *golden rule* since about the seventeenth century: do to others whatever you would want them to do to you. The verse adds, "for this is the law and the prophets," which means that this one rule sums up the Hebrew scriptures. Luke 6:31 has the same saying in the Sermon on the Plain. The saying is phrased positively: do. Other versions of the rule, older and later, are phrased negatively: do not do to others what you would hate.

The negative form is well known in Jewish sources. The book of Tobit, in the Apocrypha, says not to do to anyone what you hate (Tobit 4:15). The Talmud tells of a non-Jew who asked the teacher Hillel, a generation before Jesus, to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot. Hillel answered: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor; that is the whole Torah, and the rest is commentary, go and learn (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a). Confucius in China gave a negative form centuries earlier. Some Christian writers once claimed the positive form was superior; most scholars today see the two forms as expressing the same principle.

The sermon ends with a short *parable*, a story that teaches by comparison. Matthew 7:24–27: whoever hears these words and does them is like a wise man who built his house on rock; rain fell, floods came, winds blew, and the house stood. Whoever hears and does not do them is like a foolish man who built on sand, and that house fell with a great crash. Luke 6:47–49 tells the same story with a builder who dug deep for a foundation. The point is the same: hearing is not enough.

Matthew 7:28–29 says the crowds were astonished, because Jesus taught with authority and not like their scribes. A scribe, a trained copyist and teacher of the law, would normally cite earlier teachers for support. The sermon has cited scripture and then said "but I say to you." That is the claim the crowds heard. Christians believe that authority was real and divine; Jewish tradition has generally read Jesus as one Jewish teacher among many; historians describe the claim and study how it was heard.

words.d: the saying to treat others as you would want to be treated (Matthew 7:12, Luke 6:31); found in negative form in many traditions
a short story that teaches by comparison, usually from everyday life, and often ends with a surprise
in the gospels, a trained copyist and teacher of the law of Moses

look.title: The Rule in the King James Version
look.text: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
look.prompt: Rewrite the verse in your own words. Then compare it with Hillel's version in Shabbat 31a: what is the same, and does saying "do" instead of "do not do" change what a person is asked for?

check.q: Which teacher, according to the Talmud, summed up the whole Torah as "what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor"?
check.why: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a, gives this answer to Hillel. Confucius gave a similar rule in China, but the Talmud story is about Hillel.

check.q: What is the point of the parable of the two builders?
choices: Wealth lets people build better houses
Hearing the teaching is not enough; one must act on it
Stone houses are holier than houses of sand
check.why: Matthew 7:24–27 contrasts a hearer who does the words with a hearer who does not. Doing, not building material, is the lesson.

check.q: Why, according to Matthew 7:29, were the crowds astonished?
choices: Because the sermon was very long
Because Jesus taught with authority, unlike the scribes
Because Jesus quoted no scripture at all
check.why: The text says he taught as one having authority and not as the scribes, who cited earlier teachers. The sermon does quote scripture, so the last choice is wrong.

lessons.title: Mountain and Plain Compared
lessons.mainIdea: Luke 6:17–49 contains a shorter sermon on level ground with much of the same material as Matthew 5–7, and the differences show each gospel's choices.
reading: Luke 6:17 says Jesus came down with his disciples and stood on a level place, and there taught a great crowd. The speech that follows, Luke 6:20–49, is called the *Sermon on the Plain*. It is about thirty verses long against Matthew's hundred and eleven. It contains beatitudes, the command to love enemies, the golden rule, the saying about judging, the tree known by its fruit, and the two builders. It leaves out the antitheses, the Lord's Prayer and the teaching on giving, praying and fasting, which Luke places elsewhere or omits.

Why two sermons? Readers have answered in different ways. Some Christians, from the early church onward, have held that Jesus gave two similar sermons on two occasions. Most modern scholars think Matthew and Luke drew on a shared collection of sayings, which they call *Q* from the German word Quelle, source, and that each evangelist arranged it in his own way. On this view, Matthew built a long sermon that opens his account of Jesus's teaching; Luke kept a shorter one and spread the rest through his travel narrative.

The differences are instructive rather than random. Matthew's sermon is addressed to disciples in front of a crowd and is concerned with the law: fulfilling it, extending it, summing it up. Luke's sermon is addressed to disciples and "a great multitude of people" from Judea, Jerusalem and the coast of Tyre and Sidon, which includes non-Jewish territory. Luke's gospel as a whole is interested in the poor, in outsiders and in the reversal of fortune, and his sermon shows it.

Comparing the two versions is the basic tool of close reading in the gospels. Scholars lay the texts side by side in a *synopsis*, a book that prints parallel passages in columns. Doing so lets a reader see what each writer kept, added, reordered or dropped. That does not settle which version is older or closer to what Jesus said; it shows the shape of each gospel's choices. Chapter 32 will use the same method on the Passion narratives.

words.d: the shorter sermon of Jesus in Luke 6:20–49, delivered on level ground, that parallels much of Matthew 5–7
the hypothetical collection of Jesus's sayings that many scholars think Matthew and Luke both used; from the German Quelle, source
a book that prints parallel gospel passages in side-by-side columns for comparison

look.title: Two Sermons by the Numbers
look.cite: Verse counts from the King James Version (1611); Beatitudes Matthew 5:3–12, Luke 6:20–26
look.prompt: Luke has four blessings and four woes; Matthew has nine blessings and no woes. What might each writer gain from the shape he chose?

check.q: Where does Luke say Jesus delivered his sermon?
choices: From a boat on the lake
check.why: Luke 6:17 says Jesus stood on a level place, which is why readers call it the Sermon on the Plain. Matthew's sermon is on a mountain.

check.q: What do most modern scholars mean by Q?
choices: A lost gospel written by the apostle Quintus
A collection of Jesus's sayings that Matthew and Luke both used
The name of Luke's first reader
check.why: Q, from the German Quelle, is the hypothetical sayings source behind the material Matthew and Luke share but Mark lacks. It is a scholarly theory, not a surviving book.

check.q: Which of these appears in Matthew's sermon but not in Luke's Sermon on the Plain?
check.why: Luke places the Lord's Prayer in chapter 11, not in the sermon. The golden rule, love of enemies and the two builders are in both sermons.

lessons.title: Blessed Are the Poor, Woe to the Rich
lessons.mainIdea: Luke's beatitudes bless the poor and hungry without qualification and add four woes, which gives his sermon a sharper edge than Matthew's.
reading: Matthew 5:3 blesses "the poor in spirit." Luke 6:20 blesses "the poor." Matthew 5:6 blesses those who hunger and thirst "for righteousness." Luke 6:21 blesses those who "hunger now." Two words in Matthew and one in Luke change the meaning. Matthew's blessings can be read as describing an inner attitude, humility and longing for justice. Luke's describe a social condition: having no money and no food. Readers have argued for centuries about which is closer to the original saying.

Luke then does something Matthew's sermon does not. After four blessings he gives four *woes*: woe to you who are rich, who are full, who laugh, and of whom everyone speaks well. A woe is a form from the Hebrew prophets, a cry of warning or grief, as in Amos 6:1 and Isaiah 5:8. Luke's Jesus speaks like a prophet announcing a reversal. This fits Luke as a whole. In Luke 1 Mary sings that God has brought down the mighty and lifted the lowly, filled the hungry and sent the rich away empty (Luke 1:52–53).

Both readings have shaped Christian life. Liberation theologians in Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s, such as Gustavo Gutiérrez, read Luke's version as God's *preferential option for the poor*, a claim that the text puts God on the side of the poor. Other Christians read Matthew's "poor in spirit" as the primary meaning and understand the blessing as spiritual humility open to anyone. Neither reading erases the other verse; the two gospels keep both in the canon.

For a student of the text, the lesson is about method. A single English word, poor, can carry a whole social theology or a spiritual one depending on two words that follow it. Comparing the versions does not tell you which is right. It shows you what each writer chose to say, and it warns you against quoting one gospel as if it were all four.

words.d: a cry of warning or grief used by the Hebrew prophets and by Luke's Jesus: "woe to you who are rich"
a phrase from Catholic liberation theology for the reading that God's concern is especially for the poor
a pattern in Luke's gospel in which the low are lifted and the high brought down

look.title: One Blessing in Two Gospels

choices: Luke blesses "the poor," Matthew "the poor in spirit"
Luke blesses the rich, Matthew the poor
Luke places it at the end of the sermon

check.q: The "woe" form in Luke's sermon comes from which earlier literature?
check.why: Woes are cries of warning in prophets such as Amos and Isaiah. Luke's Jesus uses the same form.

check.q: Which reading of the beatitudes did liberation theologians such as Gutiérrez build on?
choices: Matthew's "poor in spirit" as inner humility
The doxology of the Lord's Prayer
The two builders as a lesson on housing
Luke's blessing of the poor and woe to the rich as a social reversal

lessons.title: Seed on Four Kinds of Ground
lessons.mainIdea: The parable of the sower appears in Mark, Matthew and Luke with an explanation attached, and it introduces both the form of the parable and a puzzle about why Jesus used it.
reading: Mark 4 opens with Jesus teaching from a boat to a crowd on the shore. A sower goes out to sow. Seed falls on the path and birds eat it; on rocky ground, where it sprouts and withers; among thorns, which choke it; and on good soil, where it yields thirty, sixty and a hundred times over. The story is the *parable* of the sower. Matthew 13 and Luke 8 tell it too. In all three the disciples ask what it means, and Jesus explains: the seed is the word, and the four soils are four kinds of hearer.

The Hebrew word behind the Greek word parable is *mashal*, which covers proverbs, riddles and short comparison stories. The prophet Nathan tells King David a mashal about a rich man who steals a poor man's one lamb, and David condemns the rich man before realizing the story is about himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7). That is the pattern: a story from ordinary life that pulls the listener in and then turns. Rabbis of the following centuries told thousands of such stories, often beginning "a parable: to what is the matter like?"

Between the sower and its explanation stands a hard saying. In Mark 4:11–12 Jesus tells the disciples that they have been given the secret of the kingdom, but for those outside everything comes in parables, so that seeing they may not perceive and hearing they may not understand. The words echo Isaiah 6:9–10. Readers have long puzzled over this. Does it mean parables were meant to hide? Matthew 13:13 softens it to "because" they do not see. Many scholars think Mark is explaining, after the fact, why so many did not accept the message.

Most parables in the gospels come without an explanation. The sower is unusual in having one, and some scholars think the explanation, which reads like a sermon on the story, was added by the early church. Others hold that Jesus explained his own stories to his followers. Either way, the sower shows how the gospels treat parables: as stories about the kingdom of God that reward the hearer who keeps listening.

words.d: a short comparison story from everyday life that carries a lesson and often a surprise; the gospels record about forty
the Hebrew term for a proverb, riddle or comparison story; the word behind the Greek parabole
the rule or reign of God that Jesus announces in the gospels; Matthew usually says kingdom of heaven

look.title: Nathan's Parable and the Sower
look.text: 2 Samuel 12 (paraphrased): a rich man with many flocks takes a poor man's one pet lamb to feed a guest. David, hearing it, cries that the rich man deserves to die. Nathan says: you are the man. Mark 4 (paraphrased): a sower's seed falls on a path, on rock, among thorns and on good soil; only the last bears fruit. The disciples ask what it means; Jesus says the seed is the word and the soils are hearers.

check.q: What does Jesus say the seed stands for in the explanation of the sower?
check.why: Mark 4:14 says the sower sows the word. The four soils are kinds of hearers of that word.

check.q: What is a mashal?
choices: A Greek word for a written gospel
A Roman coin used in Judea
A Hebrew term for a proverb, riddle or comparison story
The name of the boat in Mark 4
check.why: Mashal is the Hebrew word for proverbs and comparison stories, the form behind the gospel parable. Nathan's story to David is one.

check.q: Mark 4:11–12 says parables are given so that outsiders may not understand. Which prophet's words does that echo?
check.why: The lines quote Isaiah 6:9–10. Nathan told a parable but is not the source of these words.

lessons.title: Who Is My Neighbor?
lessons.mainIdea: The Good Samaritan turns the question "who is my neighbor?" into "who acted as a neighbor?" and makes a member of a despised group the hero.
reading: The story that opened this chapter is found only in Luke 10:25–37. Three men pass a wounded traveler. The first two are a priest and a Levite, both from the tribe that served in the Jerusalem temple. The third is a *Samaritan*. Samaritans lived in the hill country between Judea and Galilee, worshiped the God of Israel on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem, and kept their own version of the Torah. Jews and Samaritans in the first century treated each other as heretics; John 4:9 says plainly that Jews did not share things with Samaritans.

A first-century Jewish listener would expect the third traveler to be an ordinary Israelite, a layperson, after two clergy. Making him a Samaritan is the parable's shock. Readers have often guessed that the priest and Levite feared touching a corpse, which would make them ritually unclean; the text does not say so, and Jewish law required saving life over purity. The story does not explain their motives. It simply shows who stopped.

The ending is a *reversal* of the question. The lawyer asked who counts as a neighbor, a question about the limits of duty. Jesus asks which of the three was a neighbor, a question about behavior. The lawyer answers, "the one who showed mercy," without saying the word Samaritan. The story defines neighbor by what a person does, not by who they are. Christians have read it as the heart of Jesus's ethics; Jewish readers note that Leviticus 19:34 already commands love of the stranger, and that the parable stands within that tradition.

The Good Samaritan has become a phrase in ordinary English for anyone who helps a stranger. Many U.S. states, including Illinois, have Good Samaritan laws that protect people who give emergency help from being sued. Martin Luther King Jr., in his last speech in Memphis on April 3, 1968, retold the parable and said the priest and Levite asked what would happen to them if they stopped, while the Samaritan asked what would happen to the wounded man if he did not.

words.d: a member of a people living between Judea and Galilee who worshiped the God of Israel on Mount Gerizim; Jews and Samaritans were hostile in the first century
a member of the tribe of Levi, which served in the Jerusalem temple
the turn at the end of a parable that overturns what the listener expected

look.title: The Question Turned Around
look.text: Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
look.prompt: The lawyer asked "who is my neighbor?" Jesus asks "who was a neighbor?" Explain the difference between the two questions in your own words. Why might the lawyer avoid saying "the Samaritan"?

check.q: Which gospel contains the parable of the Good Samaritan?
check.why: The parable is found only in Luke 10:25–37. John 4 mentions Samaritans but does not tell this story.

check.q: Why is the Samaritan's role in the story a surprise to a first-century Jewish listener?
choices: Samaritans were wealthy and rarely walked
Jews and Samaritans were hostile and saw each other as worshiping wrongly
check.why: The two peoples worshiped at different mountains and kept apart. The listener expected an ordinary Israelite after a priest and a Levite, not a Samaritan hero.

check.q: How does the parable change the lawyer's question?
choices: From "who is my neighbor?" to "who acted as a neighbor?"
From "who is my neighbor?" to "where is Jericho?"
From "what must I do?" to "what must I believe?"
From a question about the law to a question about the temple
check.why: Jesus asks which of the three was a neighbor, turning a question about limits into a question about conduct.

lessons.title: A Father and Two Sons
lessons.mainIdea: The parable of the prodigal son ends without telling whether the elder brother comes in, leaving the listener to finish the story.
reading: Luke 15 holds three parables about lost things: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son. Luke says Jesus told them because religious leaders complained that he ate with tax collectors and sinners. The third story, Luke 15:11–32, is the longest parable in the gospels. A younger son asks for his share of the inheritance, goes to a far country, wastes it, and ends up feeding pigs, animals that the Torah calls unclean (Leviticus 11:7). Starving, he decides to go home and ask to be a hired servant.

The father sees him from far off, runs to him, and orders a robe, a ring, sandals and a feast. The son's prepared speech is cut short. Christians have traditionally called this the parable of the *prodigal* son, from a word meaning wasteful; many modern readers call it the parable of the forgiving father, because the father is the figure who acts. Christians read the father as an image of God's welcome to the repentant, and the story is read in many churches during Lent.

The story does not end at the feast. The elder son, coming from the field, hears music, learns the reason, and refuses to go in. He has served for years and never been given even a young goat. The father comes out to him too and says: you are always with me, and all that I have is yours; but it was right to celebrate, because your brother was dead and is alive. The parable stops there. Whether the elder brother goes in is never told.

The open ending is the parable's method. Luke's audience of complaining leaders is placed in the elder brother's shoes and left to decide. Jewish readers have noted that the father's welcome fits the Hebrew Bible's picture of a God who receives the one who returns, as in Hosea 14 and Jonah 3. Some scholars also read the story politically, as a picture of Israel and outsiders; others warn against reading the elder brother as a stand-in for Judaism, a reading that has fed hostility in the past. The text itself names no nations, only a family.

words.d: recklessly wasteful; the traditional name for the younger son in Luke 15
in the Torah, an animal or condition that is not permitted for eating or for entering sacred space; pigs are unclean (Leviticus 11:7)
a story that stops before its last question is answered, so the listener must finish it

look.title: Three Lost Things
look.text: Luke 15 (paraphrased): a shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one, and calls his friends to rejoice. A woman sweeps her house for one lost coin out of ten, and calls her neighbors to rejoice. A father welcomes a son who wasted his inheritance, and holds a feast; the elder son stands outside. Each story ends with a celebration. Only the third has someone who refuses to join it.
look.prompt: Why might Luke build to the third story? What does the elder brother add that the sheep and the coin could not?

check.q: Why, according to Luke 15:1–2, did Jesus tell the three parables of lost things?
choices: A disciple asked how to pray
Leaders complained that he ate with tax collectors and sinners
A lawyer asked who his neighbor was
The crowd asked for a sign
check.why: Luke frames the chapter with the complaint about Jesus's company. The lawyer's question is in Luke 10, and the prayer request in Luke 11.

check.q: What detail shows the younger son has reached the lowest point a Jewish listener could imagine?
choices: He works as a hired servant
He feeds pigs, animals the Torah calls unclean
check.why: Feeding pigs, unclean under Leviticus 11:7, marks the depth of his fall. He only wishes to become a hired servant; he is not one yet.

check.q: How does the parable of the two sons end?
choices: The elder brother joins the feast
The father sends the elder brother away
It stops before saying whether the elder brother goes in
check.why: The story ends with the father's words to the elder son. The text never says what he decides.

lessons.title: The Last Shall Be First
lessons.mainIdea: The laborers in the vineyard, found only in Matthew, pays every worker the same and asks the hearer whether generosity can feel unfair.
reading: Matthew 20:1–16 tells of a landowner who hires workers for his vineyard at dawn, agreeing on a *denarius*, a Roman silver coin that was a common day's wage. He hires more at nine, at noon, at three, and at five in the afternoon. At evening he pays the last group first, and gives them a full denarius. Those hired at dawn expect more and get the same. They grumble. The owner answers: I did you no wrong; you agreed to a denarius; may I not do what I choose with what is mine? Is your eye evil because I am good?

The story ends with a saying that also appears just before it (Matthew 19:30): so the last shall be first, and the first last. The parable illustrates the saying, but the illustration is uncomfortable. Every reader who has held a job feels the dawn workers' complaint. Nothing in the story says the owner was unjust; everyone received what was promised. The sting is that equal pay for unequal work feels wrong even when no one is cheated. That discomfort is the point the parable presses.

Christians have read the vineyard in several ways. Early readers took the hours as stages of history or of a life, with the late workers as those who come to faith late. Others read it as Matthew's word to Jewish followers of Jesus who had kept the law all their lives and now saw Gentiles, non-Jews, welcomed on equal terms. Many modern readers see a teaching about *grace*, favor that is given rather than earned. Jewish sources have a similar story: a rabbinic parable in the Jerusalem Talmud tells of a king who paid a short-time worker a full wage because he had done more in two hours than others did all day.

Parables like this one show how the form works. A familiar scene, a vineyard at harvest, is set up with care. Then one detail, the order and equality of payment, breaks the pattern. The listener's reaction, whether outrage or relief, becomes part of the meaning. Scholars such as C. H. Dodd described a parable as a story that leaves the mind in enough doubt to tease it into active thought. That is a description of how these stories work, whatever a reader decides they mean.

words.d: a Roman silver coin, a common day's wage for a laborer in the first century
in Christian usage, favor or forgiveness given freely rather than earned
a person who is not Jewish; in the New Testament, the nations outside Israel

A jar used for storing wine
A tax paid to the temple
check.why: The denarius was a Roman silver coin commonly paid for a day's labor, which is the wage agreed in Matthew 20.

The late workers are paid less

sections.title: The Kingdom and a Neighboring Teacher

lessons.title: What the Kingdom Means
lessons.mainIdea: "Kingdom of God" is the central phrase of Jesus's teaching in the first three gospels, and readers have long debated whether it means a present reality, a coming one, or both.
reading: Mark 1:15 gives the first words of Jesus in that gospel: the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe the good news. Matthew usually writes *kingdom of heaven* instead, using heaven as a respectful way to avoid saying God, a common Jewish practice. The two phrases mean the same thing. The Greek word basileia means a reign or rule more than a territory. Most of the parables begin by saying what the kingdom is like: a seed, yeast, a treasure, a pearl, a net, a feast.

The idea has roots in the Hebrew Bible, where God is called king (Psalm 47, Isaiah 52:7) and the prophets look for a day when God's rule will be plain to all. Jewish prayers of the period, like the Kaddish, ask for that kingdom to come. Jesus does not define the term; he assumes his hearers know it and tells stories about it. That is one reason readers have disagreed about what he meant.

Three readings have dominated modern scholarship. Some, following Albert Schweitzer in 1906, read the kingdom as *eschatological*, a coming end of the present age that Jesus expected soon. Others, following C. H. Dodd in the 1930s, read it as already present in Jesus's work: Luke 17:21 says the kingdom is within, or among, you. Most scholars today hold some form of both: the kingdom in the gospels is already at work and not yet complete. Christians across traditions pray for it to come and also speak of living in it now.

Jewish and Christian expectations differ here. Judaism has generally looked for God's kingdom as a future age of peace, with the messiah as its human king, and has not seen it as having arrived. Christians believe the kingdom began with Jesus and will be completed at his return. Both draw on the same prophets. A student can describe this difference precisely without deciding it, and precision is what the sources require: which text, which phrase, which reader.

words.d: Matthew's usual phrase for the kingdom of God, using heaven as a respectful substitute for the divine name
having to do with the end of the present age; the eschatological reading sees the kingdom as a coming end-time event
from the Hebrew for anointed one; in Jewish hope a future king who brings God's peace, and for Christians a title of Jesus

Heaven was a respectful substitute for the divine name in Jewish usage
Matthew wanted to avoid Mark's wording for legal reasons
check.why: Avoiding the name of God by saying heaven was a common Jewish practice. The two phrases mean the same.

check.q: What did Albert Schweitzer's 1906 reading of the kingdom emphasize?

The kingdom as the Roman Empire
The kingdom as the church in Rome
The kingdom as a code of table manners
check.why: Schweitzer read the kingdom eschatologically, as an imminent end-time event. Dodd later stressed the kingdom as present.

check.q: How do Jewish and Christian expectations of God's kingdom generally differ?
choices: Judaism denies God is king; Christianity affirms it
Both hold that the kingdom arrived in the first century

check.why: Both draw on the prophets and both call God king. They differ on whether the kingdom has begun with Jesus.

lessons.title: Hillel and Jesus
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel, a Jewish teacher a generation before Jesus, left sayings that sound close to the gospels, and setting the two side by side shows Jesus's teaching within first-century Judaism.
reading: *Hillel* was a Jewish teacher active in Jerusalem around the end of the first century BCE. Tradition says he came from Babylonia, was poor as a student, and became head of a school whose rulings usually favored the more lenient reading of the law. His rival Shammai led a stricter school. The Mishnah, compiled around 200 CE, and the Talmud preserve sayings attributed to him. He died, by traditional dating, about 10 CE, when Jesus was a child.

The tractate *Pirkei Avot*, Sayings of the Fathers, records Hillel saying: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And when I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? (Avot 1:14). It also records him saying: be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and bringing them near to the Torah (Avot 1:12). Beside them, the Talmud's story of the whole Torah on one foot, with its golden rule, is his most famous saying.

Set Hillel's sayings beside the sermon and the likeness is plain: a golden rule, a call to be a peacemaker, love of people, the Torah summed up in a sentence. Jewish scholars such as Joseph Klausner in the 1920s and, later, Geza Vermes and Amy-Jill Levine have read Jesus as a Jewish teacher of the same world, whose sayings belong in that conversation. Many Christian scholars agree, and treat the parallels as evidence of a shared tradition rather than of borrowing in either direction.

The differences matter as much as the likeness. Hillel's sayings are preserved as rulings and maxims in a legal tradition; the gospels present Jesus's sayings inside a narrative that ends in his death and, Christians believe, his resurrection. Jewish tradition remembers Hillel as one of its founding teachers; Christian tradition remembers Jesus as far more than a teacher. Reading the two together is not a way to blend them. It is a way to see the first-century Jewish world both belonged to.

words.d: a leading Jewish teacher in Jerusalem around the turn of the era, known for lenient rulings and for the golden rule in Shabbat 31a
Sayings of the Fathers, a tractate of the Mishnah that collects the ethical sayings of early rabbis
the first written collection of rabbinic law and teaching, compiled around 200 CE

chapters.title: Passion, Resurrection and the Historical Jesus
chapters.bigQuestion: When four accounts of the same days differ, what can a reader learn from the differences, and what can a historian say about the man behind them?

story.title: Four Columns on One Table
story.kicker: A class lays the last chapters of four gospels side by side and starts counting what matches and what does not.
paragraphs: The teacher hands out four photocopies and a highlighter. Each sheet holds the story of one Friday: Mark 14–15, Matthew 26–27, Luke 22–23, John 18–19. The students tape them to the table in four columns, in the order most scholars think they were written, Mark first. The task is simple. Highlight every sentence that appears in all four. Then mark what appears in only one.

The columns fill with color fast. A supper. A garden. An arrest at night. A hearing before the high priest, then a hearing before Pilate, the Roman governor. A crowd. A man named Barabbas released. A cross outside the city, two others crucified alongside, a sign over the head, a burial before sundown. All four have these. The order is almost the same. The students expected more disagreement than this.

Then the single-column marks begin. Only Luke sends Jesus to King Herod for a hearing. Only Matthew tells of Pilate's wife's dream and Pilate washing his hands. Only John records a long conversation between Jesus and Pilate that ends with the governor asking, "What is truth?" The last words from the cross differ: Mark and Matthew give one saying, Luke three different ones, John three others. The sign over the cross is worded four ways.

A student asks the obvious question. Which one is right? The teacher answers with another question. Right about what? If the question is what a Roman execution looked like, historians can say a good deal. If the question is what the death of Jesus means, that is what each gospel is answering, and each answers in its own way. A reader can hold both questions at once, as long as she knows which one she is asking.

This chapter does what the class did. It reads the four Passion narratives together, then the accounts of the empty tomb and the resurrection, which Christians hold as the center of their faith. It then turns to the historian's question: what can be known about Jesus of Nazareth from sources inside and outside the New Testament? Finally it looks at how Jews and Muslims have understood Jesus, and how a person can study a text that others, or they themselves, believe.
story.think: The four accounts agree on the order of events and differ in details and sayings. What kinds of questions would the agreement help answer, and what kinds would the differences help answer?

lessons.title: Reading in Four Columns
lessons.mainIdea: The Passion narratives are the longest continuous stories in the gospels, and reading them side by side is the standard method for seeing what each writer chose.
reading: The *Passion* is the Christian name for the suffering and death of Jesus, from the Latin word for suffering. Each gospel devotes about two chapters to the last day, far more space than to any other single day. Many scholars think the Passion narrative was the first part of the Jesus story to be told as a connected account, before the gospels were written, because the four agree so closely on its order. The rest of each gospel is arranged more freely.

The four gospels are not four independent reports. Most scholars date Mark first, around 70 CE, and think Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source, adding material of their own. These three are called the *Synoptic Gospels*, from a Greek word meaning seen together, because they can be laid in parallel columns. John, usually dated around 90 to 100 CE, tells the story in a different order with long speeches and few parables, and many scholars think it was written without direct use of the other three.

None of the gospels names its author in the text. The names Matthew, Mark, Luke and John come from titles attached in the second century, and church tradition identifies them with two apostles and two companions of apostles. Many scholars treat the authors as unknown early Christians writing for particular communities. This course uses the traditional names as labels for the books, as scholars of all views do.

Reading in columns has a name: *redaction criticism*, the study of how each editor, or redactor, shaped shared material. When Matthew keeps a scene from Mark but adds a line, or Luke drops one, the change is evidence of that writer's concerns. The method does not tell a reader what happened. It shows what each gospel wants its reader to see, which is a different and answerable question.

words.d: the suffering and death of Jesus as the gospels tell it; from the Latin for suffering
Matthew, Mark and Luke, which share so much material that they can be seen together in parallel columns
the study of how each gospel writer edited and arranged shared material to express his own concerns
